lead: Dutch painter (1632-1675) from Delft, with about three dozen surviving paintings; his color is calm light on yellow, blue and pearl-grey.
paras: Johannes Vermeer lived and worked in Delft and left very few paintings, about three dozen. His interiors with a single window are among the best-known pictures of the Dutch Golden Age.

His blues were costly. Ball reports that natural ultramarine, made from lapis lazuli, cost 45 guilders an ounce in 1626, and Vermeer kept using it, as in The Milkmaid of about 1658. Gage points out that yellow and blue dominate his palette, a coincidence with the then-new theory that those two colors make white light.

Finlay says, with some uncertainty, that his luminous whites may include grains of alabaster and quartz. The forger Han van Meegeren was caught partly because his fake Vermeer used cobalt blue; cobalt blue was not invented until long after Vermeer.
Look at how the shadows are colored: a pale wall near a window carries yellow and blue in softer measures, not grey.

Our archive holds 43 Vermeer paintings, photographs of varnished panels and canvases, so these are approximate. The color he uses most beyond his peers is Smoky Black, in 29 of 43 paintings at about three times the usual rate, followed by Black and a dark olive brown. Smoky Black is also his darkest large area, covering at least 3% of 25 canvases.
